utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Unfortunately, the Chamber was not able to sit until now because the previous trial ran over time; it's regrettable. Sir, Mr. Simic, if I could remind you of the affirmation that you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, could we please have 65 ter number 3D22 shown on the screen. I've got hard copies in English for assistance of the Court which sometimes is better than the electronic version. If they could be handed forward, I would be very grateful. Your Honour, I don't have anything on the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We would need to have the document ID rather than the 65 ter number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, what I have got is ET 04675901 to 5902. Your Honour, I'm told that it's a Sljivancanin document originally. The reference we have is 3D050215. Does that help?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, can you see the screen all right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Instructions for using the military police, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, what I've got is a translation just -- I don't know if this is right. It should be JNA guidelines for application of service regulations of SFRY armed forces military police. But it's of application to the military police. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go to I'll call it paragraph 255. Can that be located, please? It may assist if it's 3D05, then it's 263 and 264. In the English version, there are two pages. So 255, have we got it? Yes. The subheading here is "escorting the prisoners of war." It's guidelines for the military police when they find themselves in such situations. That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd just like to deal with 255. I will move on, but I'm going to read it out and I hope at a speed that is acceptable to all parties. 255: "Military police participates in the escort of the more important prisoner of war from the division station where they are gathered to the prisoner of war camps. Troops appointed for the escort of prisoners of war must be well-trained." And then it goes on: "Whenever possible, people with knowledge of the language spoken by the prisoners of war shall be appointed to the escort organs." So that is the preamble. 256, I'd like to deal with this, please. "The commanding officer who orders the escort of the prisoners of war is obliged to inform the commanding officer of the unit appointed to escort on the number and the category of the prisoners of war to be escorted, the manner of the escort, the access of movement and the manner in which food and other necessities are to be supplied." Well, clearly, there is a subdivision here of command and control, because we're dealing with the commanding officer who orders the escort and he is obliged to inform the commanding officer of the unit who is escorting. Now, in this scenario from the hospital at Vukovar on the morning of the 20th of November, who was the commanding officer who ordered the escort of the prisoner of war? Can we have his name, please.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, my task was not to escort persons. My unit had the task of searching persons. As for escorting, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So are you saying to this Court that on the 20th of November, 1991, you did not know who was the commanding officer who ordered the escort? Is that actually what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you that the battalion commander gave me the task of searching these persons. I did not escort prisoners, I only searched persons. Probably when my commander received tasks, the person who gave him his tasks gave the person who was escorting these people his task as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But Paunovic never told you this in your briefing. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He told me only the task of searching persons. Escorting, I was not involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what about the person who was escorting the prisoners of war? Who was responsible for that? Who was the commanding officer of -- or who was the commander of that particular task? What was his name, please?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday that Major Vukasinovic took over the persons who I had frisked. I assumed that he was the one responsible for escorting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the security organ, as far as you could see, were responsible for escorting them; is that right? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Vukasinovic then worked in the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move 256 the second paragraph, because I'm going to suggest to you that this is a guideline, maybe a duty when it comes to military police, but it's a guideline generally. "Upon receiving the escort task, the commanding officer of the escort -- or the escort unit takes the following measures, carries out a roll-call of the prisoners of war from the list received by the organs of the command, searches the prisoners of war, warns the prisoners of war through interpreters that in case of an attempted escape, they will be prevented by the use of arms." A rather polite way of saying "shot." Now, when we're talking about these three criteria, searches of prisoners of war, that's what you're doing. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So: "Carries out a roll-call of the prisoners of war." Who was carrying out the roll-call?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was carried out in the hospital. I don't know, because I was outside the hospital. I was in front of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So what you are saying is, as far as you are aware -- well, it's not a case as far as you were aware. You yourself made no list. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not make any lists, nor did I receive any lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you were not ordered to make a list and you did not make a list. So when we talk about lists around we talk about you, Mr. Simic, lists and yourself don't go together. Someone else's responsibility. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't have any lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, bearing in mind these are the guidelines for an evacuation or an escorting of prisoners of war, and bearing in mind we have heard evidence about the Mitnica evacuation where lists were compiled with some precision, who was compiling the list of these people coming out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, who went into the hospital dealing with the initial part of the evacuation? Was that Major Sljivancanin and some others?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that a group of officers, including Major Sljivancanin, entered the hospital. Now, what the organisation of work was in the hospital, who was the organiser, who was implementing it, I don't know because I didn't enter the premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I want to move on in time - we will come back - look at 258, please. Again, the guideline for the military police. Could you look up at 258? I'll read it out to assist you. "When transporting the prisoners of war by vehicles (trucks) they should be boarded so that one or two escorts board first and then a certain number of prisoners of war." So the modus operandi that was used for the buses, I think, were two soldiers, isn't that right, on each bus?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you keep asking me about escorting and transporting these people, whereas I was only responsible for the search. Now, how that was organised, how many of them were in their -- involved in the security, how many escorted them, that was not my task. I don't know anything about that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you may not know about the tasks, so you say, but you certainly know that there were soldiers on the buses; that is correct. You saw them, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And as far as you could see, it would conform with 258, that there were soldiers on the bus for control. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, you were able to see the buses, because you've told us that in evidence. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But it's also right to say you weren't able to see the buses every second of every minute, but you saw them over a period of time. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's look, then, at the next paragraph of 258: I read: "The commanding officer of the escort," or "the escort unit, controls the boarding, checks the disposition of the escorts, and the prisoners of war on every vehicle and the regularity of" -- there's a difficulty in the translation: "The place next to the driver in the first vehicle." Well, clearly there is reference to the commanding officer of the escort unit. You were able to see the buses. I would like to know, then, please, who you considered was the commanding officer of the escort unit? So can you tell us a name, please? That you considered was in that position, not what you know, of course, but what you considered, from what you saw?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday as well that I had assumed that it was Major Ljubisa Vukasinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In fairness to you, I think you've said you were doing a lot of things, so you weren't able to see the bus all the time. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And therefore, you cannot say whether Major Sljivancanin was at the bus at some time when you were not looking at it. That is correct also, logically, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us then move, please, to 260 and 261. "When the prisoners of war are escorted through the zone of combat activities," this escort was supposed to be going to Sremska Mitrovica, "the commanding officer of the escort is obliged to leave it as soon as possible, shorten the depth of the column, avoid the movement in the area which facilitates the escape and in the regions where infiltrated or remaining enemy groups activities have been felt." 261: "Following the completion of the escort, the prisoner of war are handed over to the prisoner of war command when the commanding officer of the escort patrol (escort unit) takes a confirmation note on the hand-over of the prisoners of war, their belongings and their money. The confirmation note is then handed over to the commanding officer who ordered the escort to take place." Now, 261 basically creates a circle of command because what is being suggested in 256 about commanding officer and the commanding officer of the unit to escort ensures that you have a full circle of command, so you count them all out and you count them all back in. That's right, isn't it? That's the whole purpose.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, what it says in item 261 is all correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when we are talking about an evacuation, we're talking about the compilation of lists, a number of lists, or a list with a number of people on it, and then when it comes to the hand-over, to ensure that nobody's being taken off the bus. That, in substance, is what it means, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, then, please, to deal with one part of your statement. May I just find it. It is page 5 of the first translation. It's the B/C/S version of -- which is page 021-88241, and I hope the Court have now got the correct bundle that is correctly paginated. Have you got that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If you go to tab 2. On the English version, page 5, it is the last line: "During the search, no register was kept, nor were lists made of people taken out of the hospital and their loading onto the buses. I do not know whether anyone had kept a record in the hospital before this." Would you accept from me that if there is to be an evacuation of prisoners of war or detained persons, that it is a fundamental -- that there should be a list made of people taken away and put or detained in buses?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in my statement that in the company -- or, rather, I, as company commander, didn't keep any records. You would have to ask somebody else whether they kept any records. I didn't. I don't know whether somebody else compiled lists and made records.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I have already said that I accept that you did not make lists and that's not what I'm asking you. I am asking you as a military policeman, having seen the military police regulations, that it is a fundamental, that when you are removing people and putting them into custody, that you take a list or you compile a list of those people so you have a record of whom you have under your control. It is a fundamental, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. The rules provide for that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you were given your task by Paunovic, and it was merely the searching task, did you ask: Who is keeping the list of the people who are coming through, or do you want me to do it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him and he said that no lists needed to be compiled, that people would be taken from the hospital and that my only task was to frisk them, to confiscate any cold or fire weapons if we find them. So I did only a minor portion of that entire task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you aware that the security organ had lists of people that they wanted to speak to or investigate in relation to the matters in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you never heard of the security organ having a list or going into the hospital and using that list to isolate or identify individuals. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear any information about any lists, and I don't even know whether there were any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's axiomatic, it's obvious, is it not, that if you do not compile lists, there is always a danger that you can lose or individuals on that evacuation can be removed without record. That is correct also, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear phrases by soldiers such as: These are dead men; or, They should be swallowed by the night? Did you ever hear any soldiers saying that about the people who were being taken out to the buses?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: A battalion of military police, I believe, is not the normal size of a battalion, which is around about 600 or 700 men. A battalion of military police, I believe, is around about 150 men. Is that correct or not? In 1991, I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Battalion of the military police was supposed to have about 500 people in the establishment terms, and at the beginning of the war, that's how strong it was. Yesterday I gave you the reasons for the decrease in the number of troops, and I told you that my company initially had over 100 men, and then later on we were down to 48 men. As for total numerical strength of the battalion at the end of combat operation, I truly don't know what it was. I don't know how many people there were in other companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that your understanding, although you say you hadn't heard about it directly, your understanding was that this evacuation was going to go to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not told exactly the place where they were supposed to be taken. The people who were there, I heard from them that Sremska Mitrovica was mentioned. I can tell you that I even joked with them saying that perhaps I should go with them in order to reach Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But there was no suggestion of them stopping for a government meeting, was there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was not aware that there was any cabinet session in progress or that they were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you were not aware, were you, that they were going to be stopped at the JNA barracks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I only overheard that Sremska Mitrovica was being mentioned. I repeat: I did not receive any tasks related to the transportation of these people. I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to move on to a different topic. My last question on this one is: To whom did the soldiers belong who were in the buses, to what unit?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which unit they were from, but I know that they were not from my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, please, to turn to your tab 4; the English is tab 3. Now, you have dealt with this topic already but I just want to top and tail it a little, if I may. I'd like, if the Court would be kind enough please to turn to English page 9; the B/C/S is 0461-9788. It's a question from the presiding judge. It reads as follows, the top of page 9: "From the moment when you secured the hospital from the outside, did any people, anyone from the outside enter the hospital, soldiers, officers, civilians, were there attempts to enter the hospital?" Now, clearly that question relates not only to the 20th but it also relates to the 19th of November, because you say you secured the hospital on the 19th and then the 20th. This is your reply: "There was a very large crowd around the hospital. Someone heard that so-and-so who had killed his brother was inside, another that so-and-so had set his house on fire. People were trying to enter to mete out justice on their own." Now, what did you mean by the phrase -- I see there is an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a minor intervention. I think it would be fair to the witness if the Prosecutor, when reading the statement given by the witness, would read absolutely everything. But after the first question of the president of the chamber, there is a different answer provided by Mr. Simic in the original. First he said no, and then the rest of the text followed. And I think that it would be fair if the text would be put to the witness in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I must confess, I missed the word "no," so my apologies for that; that's just my eyesight. So Mr. Simic: "Answer: No." And then: "There was a very large crowd around the hospital -- someone heard that so-and-so who had killed his brother was inside, another that so-and-so had set his house on fire -- people were trying to enter to mete out justice on their own." What do you mean, "people were trying to enter to mete out justice on their own"? What does that phrase mean?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was their term. They wanted to mete out justice; that's how they phrased it. Now, whether they had a trial in mind or something else, I truly wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But it's right, isn't it, because we have heard evidence of it, that the TO, Vukovar TO were being used to identify, to assist in the identification of individuals within the hospital. Now, what I'd like to know is: Who gave them the authority to come inside?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they took part in identifying the individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have heard evidence that they did, evidence from Mr. Sljivancanin, whom you are here to assist in giving evidence. So I would like to know who was giving them the authority to come into the hospital? Because you were in charge of the cordon of protection.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I stated that a group of people came in, a group of officers. Whether anyone among them was from the TO, I don't know. All I know is that everybody who came in was uniformed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, with the utmost kindness to you, talk about the 19th, we'll go to the 20th. On the 19th, you were there. You were the officer in charge of protecting the hospital. I will use the word "securing the hospital." That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I'm asking who gave the authority for TOs to come into that hospital compound?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps they had entered before I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But your task --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they did at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly like to ask the Prosecutor in such a case where he is putting somebody's statement to the witness, to give us references so that we can verify whether that can be found somewhere. Namely, that on the 19th, the TO had entered and that somebody stated that. Could we please have the reference. Sljivancanin did not speak in his evidence about the 19th and about the identification in the light that the Prosecutor just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will deal with it in general terms, if I may, and then deal with it specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that's fair in the circumstances, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have heard on, for example, reselection processes in the hospital, on the 20th specifically, that there were TO members there assisting on the reselection -- what I will call the reselection of individuals from the hospital. What I want to know is: Who was giving them the authority to enter, if you were in charge of the cordon?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that a group of officers had arrived. All of them were in a uniform. They entered with Major Sljivancanin. I didn't check whether all of these men were from the Guards Brigade or the TO or some other units. I simply believed that if they were present there with Major Sljivancanin, who was chief of security organ, that they had proper authorisation to enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But we have documents from ECMM monitors who said that Chetniks were seen within the ground of the hospital. And I can give the reference on that, if there's any difficulty. So did you see Chetniks within the grounds of the hospital? I think it was on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So what was the method of control for people coming in and out on the 19th, in and out of your security organ -- your security cordon? Did you have a list of people who could come in? Did you have a booking in, or was no one allowed in?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained yesterday that those who were not part of medical staff and who were not patients could leave freely, and I told you that that lasted for about an hour or two after the dark. Those who had to enter the hospital and were allowed to enter were announced by the brigade command, by the battalion commander, and that would go through me, they would call me and say such and such a person would come in, but I told you that there were not too many visitors on the 19th, a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross came and then a TV crew and Major --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name of the major, TV crew and Major -- your voice tailed away. Could you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a foreign TV crew, I think it was from SkyNews, it was brought in by Captain Maric. Yesterday I explained that procedure with that TV crew. I told you that Major Mladen Karan came to fetch Dr. Bosanac. I explained that yesterday as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But would it be right to say that in actual fact who came in and out was a matter of discretion?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, one couldn't say so. I told you just a minute ago that if somebody was supposed to come, announcement was made down the chain of command so that we would receive information that somebody was supposed to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if Major Sljivancanin arrived at the gate you wouldn't allow him in. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Major Sljivancanin was from the brigade command; therefore, he was authorised to enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did that apply to other officers of the brigade command or OG South?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the details concerning entry and exit, I really don't remember. I can tell you what the rules provide. Now, as to whether they called me, whether they sent me a list of people who were authorised to enter, I definitely don't remember that. It is possible, though, that at that point in time, there was a list of persons who were authorised to enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You told us that after your evidence in 2005 I think that you then spoke to a group of other officers to discuss this situation. Those are my words not yours. But I think that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke to people who took part in these events. My goal was to refresh our recollections, because some people remembered some details, other people remembered other details, so I thought that it would be easier for us to refresh our memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't want to discuss what was said, do you understand, but I do want to know who you were speaking to. Now, did you speak to Paunovic? Or perhaps a fairer way of putting it is, you tell us who you were speaking to, because we have already heard evidence about various things. So can you tell us the names of the people you were speaking to?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember all of the people, but now that you've mention Paunovic, yes, I talked to him, and the list is longish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, do you want to make a start in telling us who is on the first names of the list?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Todorovic, Second Lieutenant; Major Vukasinovic; Major Susic. Those would be the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There were a few more, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were people. For example, Djorja Borovcanin, he was my best man, and he was in the 2nd Assault Detachment. Sasa Bojkovski. Well, those would be the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What about Borisavljevic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I spoke to him about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You were here in The Hague from Wednesday, and of course you are what is called part heard from last night. Did you speak to anyone last night about this case?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing particular. I had a dinner together with Susic and Vukasinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And of course it's correct to say that Susic and Vukasinovic are two witnesses who are about to give evidence. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you not told by your lawyers that you should not speak to other people who are witnesses in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't discuss the case. I didn't tell them what I had stated. I simply explained the procedure concerning what happens when one enters the courtroom and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So Simic, who will be giving evidence -- Susic -- I beg your pardon. Susic, who will be giving evidence probably on Friday, and Vukasinovic, I think gives evidence next week. He's already here. When did Mr. Vukasinovic come?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Monday, Tuesday, was it? Is today Wednesday? Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So did you have dinner with Mr. Vukasinovic on Monday as well?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When did Mr. Susic come?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Came together. But they had some problems because their luggage hadn't arrived, so most of the time we talked about that luggage and we were trying to get a hold of that luggage. They didn't have anything to wear. They were nervous. We talked mostly about that luggage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you had dinner with them, I presume, on Monday and last night as well.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal with one or two other small areas. It is right, is it not, that it was known, or you certainly were aware, that there had been negotiations for an evacuation pending the fall of Vukovar. Is that right or not? That you knew what we will call the Zagreb Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, during the war, I was just a company commander, and you are asking me about some decisions that were made by the top echelons of the state. All sorts of things were talked about. I cannot remember all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I just ask you, please, the English version is page 17; the B/C/S version I hope will be 0461-9792.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I must just check, it's this pagination again. I'm going to read it out; that's the best thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's one of the replies that you made. It's on the B/C/S page number 0461-9792 and the reply that you gave is this: "Well, later there was that when everyone came on the basis of that agreement by the government of Croatia, and I don't know with whom. But at that time, we did not have any other assignments other than to provide security." On the agreement by the government of Croatia, did you not know about it at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me whether on the 17th and 18th I had heard about that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about the 20th and the 19th here. You asked me whether I heard that there were negotiations taking place during those days, the 17th and 18th, and I said no, but later on I found out. This is already the 19th or the 20th. I don't know what day it relates to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So would it be right to say that you were aware that when those people were taken away on the buses it was prior to the ICRC or the ECMM arriving? At the hospital, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about the 20th, are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think after the evacuation, the representatives of the international community came and that the Red Cross team came after that evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So there's no mistake about it, these men who were taken off on the buses, they were taken away before the ECMM and the ICRC arrived. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I think that they were taken before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would suggest you knew perfectly well that they were taken away before that and that it was a very specific plan to make sure that those people were taken away before the ECMM and the ICRC arrived. That is right, isn't it? They were going to be taken to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Sir, you are asking me about something that was outside the purview of my work then. I repeat once again that it was only the search that was the task of the company. I was told when this was supposed to begin and I know that we finished by around 10.00. Now, who decided what is something that you will have to ask these other people who are making the decisions. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Two final questions. Could we please have MFI 689. Can we turn it round. Now, we have a photograph here. I don't think it's unreasonable to say - that's fine, thank you - photograph, Mr. Sljivancanin in the middle with his arms apparently around two gentlemen. Do you know who they are?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the quality of the photograph is very poor. I cannot recognise anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I suggest the gentleman on the left is Lancuzanin, otherwise known as Kameni, and the one on the right is Stanko Vujanovic, the man who has the beard with the black hat?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This first gentleman that you mentioned, I never saw. As for Stanko Vujanovic, I knew him but this is very unclear. I cannot recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the reality is when it comes to the actual subordination of the assault detachment, you actually didn't know which TO units were subordinated to whom, if at all? You simply didn't know. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within my unit, there weren't any Territorial Defence units. I really don't know about other units in the brigade, whether there were any subordinated units of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour. May I tender two matters, the first is the 3D22. Which is the regulations for the military police. I would seek to tender that as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You mean the regulations or the two pages extract?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just the two pages extracts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Those two pages will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 856, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And finally, the photograph which is MFI -- but I think there may be an objection. Mr. Lukic, I think, objects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic -- Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, an attempt had already been made by the Prosecution to bring this photograph into evidence when Mr. Panic was questioned; Mr. Weiner tried to do that. We oppose having it admitted into evidence for the same reasons. Today you heard from the witness that quite simply he did not recognise these persons so let it remain marked for identification only, and then if somebody appears who can confirm its authenticity, and the identity of the persons in the photograph, then we can discuss that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you counter that in any way, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. Upon reflection, it's a fair objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. A good try-on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Never a try-on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Your Honours. Good afternoon to all in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, good afternoon to you as well. On the basis of the particulars you gave to the Trial Chamber, I see that today is your birthday, so may I wish you a happy birthday. That's the way it is. You're here today, so what can I say? You talked to my colleague from the Prosecution about this agreement today. Do you know anything about this agreement, who signed it, where, when, what the content is, how many articles it contains? What do you know, if anything, about this agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except for the fact that there was an agreement and that people talked, that part of the people who were taken to Croatia were returned because they did not want to have them there. I really was not involved. I'm not aware of any particular point from this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we have this back on the screen now, what was admitted into evidence, what the Prosecutor proposed, that is to say 3D050263, Exhibit 856. I think it has been admitted. Can we see that? I think that it's paragraph 255.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I'm going to ask you what escorting means. What does that particular action of escorting involve?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to remember, because I haven't been working in the military police for about 11 years now, and even when I did work in the military police, it was for a short span of time, only four years. But it is a tactical action that can be carried out either on foot or on vehicles with the aim of transferring persons who are in custody from one location to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at paragraph 255 of this exhibit. I am going to read it. It says: "The military police takes part in escorting major prisoners of war from division stations for their collection to the camp for prisoners of war." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note they did not have the text. They did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very old rule. It was written at the time when there was a regiment, a brigade, a division, an army. And then at brigade level, only a place was set up for bringing prisoners of war together at a particular location, and from that location, they were transported to the division stations. And at army level, according to the rule, it was regulated that camps for prisoners of war should be set up. So this rule could not have been carried out in our case, at least this segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In line with this rule, can the hospital be a division station?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the hospital or a hospital cannot constitute a division station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had the task of searching persons and escorting them to the buses. What you did, that is to say, searching these persons and having them over by the bus, can that action that you took constitute escorting?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Practically these people went on for 20 or 30 metres. It was only 20 or 30 metres. We can only say that they were escorted to the bus, or rather ushered to the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken you said you went to the bus only once with the group that was seen off to the bus?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I went there so that I would show these soldiers how this was supposed to be done and so that I'd see who was taking the persons in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, throughout this time, as you carried out these tasks that you were given by the battalion commander, did you do all of that in the area in front of the hospital that you described, or is this a biggish area where you were moving about?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not really understand you. Are you referring to the search?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the search, the task that you got to search people. Where were you during that search?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the search, I was incessantly from the entrance for emergencies to the gate, and I did not leave the area all that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you came to the hospital and before you set up the security, did you establish how many entrances the hospital had, and exits, too, of course?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what we could see without any kind of special search was that in the new building, the new hospital, there were two entrances. I don't know whether we later established that there were more than that, but I know that later we did establish that one could enter the new building from the old building through a tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in front of that entrance where you were searching these persons and where you saw the persons concerned go to the bus, did you see Veselin Sljivancanin ever going to the bus?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him going in and out, but I really don't know where he went.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Where was he going in and out?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entrance into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, you just see him going in and out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes, really. I mean, I had my own task and I was paying attention to that. I was not looking at others, who was going where and who was doing what.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about the other officers who came, who you did not know, did you see them going in and out of the hospital? Did you notice them somewhere around there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think that one of them just went out through this entrance taking out these people for whom the triage was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday when the Prosecutor asked you on a number of occasions about your statement, you gave two statements, and I will ask you about two dates which are relevant and I will distinguish between evacuation 1 and evacuation 2. Evacuation 1 was the one on the 19th. You came at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear what time. .

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: -- you placed your security personnel. Do you remember what -- so it was 1400 hours and then you saw Sljivancanin there and your battalion commander, Mr. Paunovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that on the 19th, Mr. Sljivancanin left the hospital before dark?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Following that, did Veselin Sljivancanin come back to the hospital on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The evacuation of civilians which you conducted on the 19th, when did it begin, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I truly don't remember. I think it began during daylight and it continued for another hour or two after it became dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, if I remember correctly, you told the Prosecutor that you knew that these people were going to Velepromet where there was a holding centre or collection centre.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke about the search at Mitnica, I said that we had been told that all of these civilians needed to be directed towards Velepromet where a collection centre, or a holding centre, had been set up. I don't know now whether this notion of Velepromet remained with me from that task or whether later I received some additional information about there being a collection centre at Velepromet. But at any rate, I knew that there was a collection centre at Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: During the evacuation, were there any officers there who took part in that process, other than you? You were obviously present and --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no need for that because everybody who wanted to leave the area was free to do that. No selection whatsoever was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that the evacuation began during daytime; and based on what you said, I concluded that Sljivancanin was there for some time. While he was there, before he left the hospital, did he in any way take part in the process of evacuation of civilians on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't remember whether he left before the evacuation or while it was in progress. I really cannot distinguish it now. I can't tell you that he was indeed there when the evacuation commenced. I don't remember that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember observing a portion of evacuation during daytime?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Veselin Sljivancanin there where the evacuation was being conducted?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly cannot answer the question. I don't know whether he was present when the evacuation started.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say that on the 19th, your battalion commander came back from the briefing, Mr. Paunovic, and told you that the evacuation would be held on the following day?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you that the command had designated somebody who would be in charge of the evacuation, who would be the main person for the evacuation? Did he tell you anything of the sort?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He just told me about my portion of the task, and he said that he would come in the morning and that everything would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Simic, did you ever attend briefings at the command of OG South?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As company commander, I went to the briefings which were held at the commands of assault detachments only.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th, when you escorted the people you had frisked to the buses, did you know where the buses were headed? Not what you overheard, not hearsay, but did somebody tell you directly where the buses were headed?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I told you that I simply overheard that, but nobody told me anything officially. Battalion commander, when giving me my task, never told me where the buses were headed; he just told me to bring people to the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's be brief. I'm asking you directly, nobody told you that, all right. You handed over these people to Major Vukasinovic, you brought them to him. Did you ask him where the buses were going?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if I had asked him, I don't remember whether he answered but I don't even remember asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor put two statements to you, two statements that you gave. Would you please now look in the set of the documents before you, a transcript of your statement given at the Belgrade Ovcara trial where you testified, which is page 7046 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- B/C/S version, English page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read the text out to you. Page 0461-9790, which is the B/C/S version; English page 13. This is what the presiding judge asked, Mr. Simic. "And your soldiers, they escorted the group which had been frisked to the bus?" Witness Simic answered: "Yes." Presiding Judge: "Did somebody guard them in the bus? Witness Milivoje Simic: "At the time, I think that Major Vukasinovic was. As far as I know, he was responsible for the transport and I handed them over to them, and I think that there was security on the buses, too. I really do not know whether there were policemen on the bus." Did I read your words accurately?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, this pertains to which date?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The 20th. Based on your answer, the one I just read out, who was responsible for the transport from the hospital onwards in these buses?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated back then and I still think that it was Major Vukasinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What do you base your answer on?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that yesterday, that out of all the people present there, he held the most senior rank. He was the person that I communicated with at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic. Now would you please look at your transcript. B/C/S page 15 of the transcript, number 0461-9798.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just respectfully object. At the moment, I'm not quite sure of the purpose of the re-examination is; is it re-examination for consistency, which I would submit is impermissible? Why would the witness be directed to his transcript if in actual fact he's being directed already to his account that he gave in Belgrade? I wonder if my learned friend could clarify what the purpose of the question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I truly regret this position that Mr. Moore has in believing that what I am asking now here is boring, the fact that I'm putting the transcript. If you remember well, yesterday even though the witness had these transcripts, Mr. Moore quoted for a good 40 minutes verbatim the words of the witness, both uttered before the military court and before the district court in Belgrade. This topic now is precisely the topic on which Mr. Moore insisted in the beginning of his cross-examination. All I'm doing is attempting to compare two statements given by this witness about the same fact and this will conclude my redirect. I see nothing boring about what I'm doing, and I believe that it is completely improper to make such objections. So by your leave, I would like to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, the word "boring" was not used in English. Something happened in the translation. That's my one defence of Mr. Moore today. Now Mr. Moore, is there anything you would want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can resolve the problem. I will instantly apologise to Mr. Moore. The translation I received was "boring," the word in Serbian is "dosadan," whereas the actual word that was uttered was "dosledan" which means "consistent." I apologise for that; I misheard the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I suspect my learned friend is merely expressing a view that other people have taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I will leave that comment, Mr. Moore. Carry on, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do the same, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, page 15 of the transcript from the Belgrade Ovcara trial. Page number 0461-9798. English version page 29. The question put by Deputy Prosecutor Dusan Knezevic: "Who was in charge of -- you said something about it, let's turn to it -- screening and organising the transport of these persons from the hospital elsewhere? "Witness Milovo Simic: As far as I'm concerned, my battalion commander was in charge, and I think that Major Sljivancanin was in charge of the entire operation." There, Mr. Simic. When this question was put to you about the transport of these persons, what did that mean to you, the transport of persons? What did you understand that to mean when you answered that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Transporting these people away from the hospital sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could that be understood by the word "transport"?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, given what you said a bit earlier, I gave you the exact quotation, you said, and it was recorded in the transcript that Major Vukasinovic was in charge of that transport; whereas here, you say that with respect to triage and transportation of these persons, Mr. Sljivancanin was in charge. Can you reconcile what this means, what -- were you laboring under misapprehension or what was it about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would submit that there is absolutely no basis for the way my learned friend puts the question. The issues, I would submit, are different. There is reference to and answers given in relation to the entire operation as opposed to merely Vukasinovic and the transport itself. And I would submit it is not a correct topic for re-examination in this form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Bulatovic, you are trying to squeeze more from the statement and the witness than I think can be justified. If there are matters about the witness's answer that you're not clear on, please put those. If you believe that any of his answers or any of his statements to the Judge have not been properly understood, you can ask him what he meant by them, but not suggest to him what he meant by them or argue to him that he probably meant something else because of some thought that occurs to you. Understand? You're going too far. I'm not stopping you from dealing with the topic if you see those things need attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just tried to put two things to the witness; namely, that he spoke differently about the same fact on two occasions. One was the transport on page 7, B/C/S version -- or, rather, page 13 where the witness said that Major Vukasinovic was in charge of the transport. Later on, within the same testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, you can say that, you can put it to the witness and get him to confirm that, but we don't want your ideas of what it is, we want his ideas. Can you understand that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. I fully accept your suggestion and I will retrace my steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, page 7 of the transcript, the Belgrade Ovcara trial, English page 13. 0461-9790. You said you were speaking of Major Vukasinovic. You said: "As far as I'm concerned, as far as I know, he was responsible for the transport." My question is: Please tell us, based on what did you make this conclusion when you stated that? Based on what parameters did you conclude this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he was the most senior officer in the vicinity of the buses, standing next to the buses. And when I came there, I handed over these people to him, precisely to him. Based on that, I concluded that he was the most responsible person with respect to that transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Simic. If that is the case, based on what did you then, when answering the Prosecutor's question, on that same day but a bit later, about transport. So the question was once again about transport, and you answered on the second occasion that Veselin Sljivancanin was in charge of the transport. English page 29. In the prosecutor's question, triage is mentioned, or screening and the organisation of transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My page 29 bears no reference to transport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Try the question at the end of 28, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how it was translated into English, but would you please answer, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't remember any longer whether I even heard the entire question because there's obviously something illogical here. On one occasion, I stated that Major Vukasinovic was in charge. What I had in mind here were the activities which were unfolding in the hospital compound. Most likely had Major Sljivancanin been responsible for the transport, he would have left with the buses. However, Major Sljivancanin remained at the hospital even after the buses left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Simic. Your Honours, just a minute, please. Your Honour, I have concluded my redirect. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Simic, you will be pleased to know you are now free to leave and to celebrate your birthday as you wish and to go home at a convenient time. The Chamber would thank you for your attendance and the assistance you've been able to give us. The Chamber will now rise for the first break and the court officer will show you out. We will resume at 20 past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, you are being given a priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's just very briefly this. Clearly we heard from the last witness that there are two other witnesses who are now present. I appreciate the difficulties that my learned friend has on time but there are nevertheless three on that team. We would be very grateful if we could have proofing notes within a reasonable time rather than perhaps the night before. With regard to Mr. Korica, we got the proofing note yesterday which related to discussions prior to our discussions. We haven't had a supplementary note as yet, but I don't want to delay the trial, and I would hope my learned friend could try and achieve that, if at all possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have to keep a very straight face saying that, Mr. Moore, when I think of some of the difficulties the Defence had with your proofing notes. Memory has softened it, has it, in time. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I wanted to hear. That's exactly what I wanted to say by argument. Your criticism, or, rather, can I say your instructions is something that I took very seriously. They have been receiving detailed proofing notes. Branko Korica is an interesting person because no one ever talked to him officially or took any statements from him, so that's why I needed to talk to him extensively and the proofing notes are rather extensive, too, for Mr. Moore. But this is a man who never testified before, which is really surprising, but we are going to do our best not to create any problems, because it's in our own interest, after all. There are three brief matters I'd like to refer to before the witness walks in. The first has to do with the witness himself. Branko Korica is 70 years old. Since we are in public session, I don't want to go into this in detail but he is a heart patient, so I told him that we can take breaks more frequently, if necessary, but he thinks that he can handle it, but I just want to tell you that before he enters the courtroom, that we have shorter breaks but more frequent breaks. Then MFI 5, the photograph that Mr. Moore is showing witnesses, the way I showed the Hadzic video. First of all, in the captions it does say in B/C/S who is on the photograph, so if Mr. Moore is going to show this photograph to other witnesses, it would only be right to delete the names, the caption. Another thing, the photograph is from the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief and 65 ter list, but it is interesting to note that the Prosecutor told us that he would show it to Mr. Sljivancanin while he gave evidence but he didn't. Not going into his own tactics, I think that it would have been the most reasonable course to take; namely, to show the photograph to the man who is actually in the picture. Thirdly, I want to talk about the end of the hearing yesterday. I was not present. I looked at the transcript. I just have two things to say on behalf of our team. Perhaps we come from a different legal system where not everything is quite clear to us and that is why we have these situations when we collide with other legal systems, but I wanted to ask you for some instructions so that we do not have some kind of controversy in the future. You probably know that when witnesses give statements to The Hague Tribunal they get a copy for themselves, and we dealt with many witnesses like that. I just want to ask you whether you are opposed to the witness having his own statement before he starts testifying. That was my interpretation that it would be right for them to have their own statements before they started testifying, but tell us what to do. I think that the point was that during the course of his testimony -- well, I mean, that's why I'm addressing you so perhaps I did not quite understand all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, last point first. There is no impropriety about a witness being shown his previous statements, having his own copy of them, having them even with him when he gives evidence. It is open, though, whether it is a Prosecution or Defence witness, it's open, though, to counsel who is to cross-examine that witness where there is an overnight or a longer break in the course of the testimony to seek directions from the Chamber about restricting the use of such statements. It only arises where the anticipated course of cross-examination is likely to be adversely affected if the witness is constantly having access. On the occasion last night, it seemed that there was a reasonable basis for Mr. Moore's concern and action was taken. I don't recall it having happened at any other time in this trial; it may have slipped my memory if it has. It happens just occasionally. It certainly is not a matter of standard practice, and it would not be a thing about which we would give a standard direction. So I would not suggest that you need to change what you are doing because of that incident, but there may be other occasions where Mr. Moore will make some application. As for breaks, we cannot have any shorter break, we now are having theoretically the shortest break that we can have, 20 minutes, to enable the things to be done that have to be done in a break, but if it's necessary to have more frequent breaks, well, then, we will do that. If somebody is ill, well, we have to keep an eye on that and clearly respond if there are signs of the process being too much of a problem. I don't think any of the other matters call for comment by me at this time. I think we should have the witness. While the witness is coming, all counsel will have noticed that we've managed to get reservations, as it were, on the use of the courtroom for full days during some days next week. When the opportunity arose, the Chamber took it in case your case is running behind time, Mr. Lukic. We want to give you every opportunity to keep to your 8th of December so that we will certainly need to know by the end of this week whether you feel you need some of the longer sitting days next week or not, because we will need to indicate to others. There's one other Chamber wanting the courtroom if we're not going to use it. But that's why it's there, to give you a little bit of extra time. So if you could keep that in mind, and we will learn from you late tomorrow or on Friday when you are clear in your mind whether we will need to sit any of the longer hours that can be sat next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I bore that in mind even when I made my own schedule for the witnesses. But nevertheless, I would like to assess things on Friday and then we will notify you. Our evaluation of the situation right now is that we are on schedule, more or less, because we really want to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Korica, good afternoon. Would you please take the card and read allowed the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please sit down. Now, Mr. Lukic is going to ask you some questions. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Korica.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us your name and surname first for the record.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I am Branko Korica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Korica, you were born in 1936 in Croatia in a village near Gospic, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I am going to talk about your career, but just tell me what is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can say that your entire career was linked to the military, to the JNA, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1953, you went to a school for non-commissioned officers in Zrenjanin, and then in 1955 you completed that school in Bileca, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were an active-duty officer until the 31st of December, 1986, when you were retired as warrant officer first class?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please pause a bit after my question, I already told you that, so that everything can be interpreted. As for most of your career, you spent it in the security organs or, rather, from 1959 all the way up to 1986 when you were, in fact, retired; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for your work in the security organs, from 1971 until you retired, you worked in the counter-intelligence group of the 1st Military District of the 1st Army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are a widower and you have one child. But I wish to underline that in that period while you worked in the counter-intelligence group of the 1st Army, for a while your heads of the counter-intelligence group were Geza Farkas, Lenko Milic and Bogdan Vujic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you remember for how long Bogdan Vujic was your superior?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Bogdan Vujic was the head, I think, say, from 1981 until 1983. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I already said that you retired in 1986. At one point in time, were you reactivated, called back into the JNA and, if so, when?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: On the 1st of January, 1991 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: On the 1st of November, 1991; interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened then? Where were you? Who were you with? How did this happen?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Three of us came there. I, Krgo Mladen, and Mitrovic Bozo. We had retired together, and we went to visit our colleagues at the command of the 1st Army. Among other people, we visited the chief of security of the army, General -- right this moment I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I guess it's initial excitement. It's Mile Babic. Everybody in this courtroom knows it and it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: After a brief conversation, the late Bozo said, since they knew each other well, as far back as from Sarajevo. He said: Comrade-general, I brought these two so that you can send them to the front line. The general took this seriously, and he said: Go straight away to the police battalion, have uniforms issued to you, and come here tomorrow morning to the army command. You, Korica, are going to Sid, to Colonel Petkovic and Grgo will stay here at the command to work on administrative affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I did my arithmetic. You were 55 years of age then, you had already retired. But tell me, at that time, were you still a reserve non-commissioned officer of the Yugoslav People's Army in view of your age?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what happened then. Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Grgo stayed at the command, and I went in a military vehicle to Sid. I reported to Colonel Petkovic who was stationed at the post office in Sid. After a brief conversation, he sent me to Captain Muncan who would be my boss, Dragan Muncan. A colleague came to pick me up from the post office and he took me to an apartment nearby where they were staying, and that is where we stayed throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, do you know what position he held at the time, Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: He was chief of security of the Operations Group centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was the seat of that organ?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: At the post office in Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that Captain Muncan was your direct superior. How many other persons, in addition to you, were there in that group?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Captain Muncan was the superior, and in addition to us, there was Captain Musesku Petar and Staff Sergeant Radakovic Nebojsa.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell us briefly what you did in Sid at the time. What you were your duties and tasks?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Initially my tasks were to conduct interviews with persons of interest to us who had been taken into custody and taken to the holding centre for further screening as well as to conduct interviews with persons who had fled from that area engulfed by war, and they were mostly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were those people brought from to the holding centre and what were -- was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Persons from all over the territory covered by war in that area were brought to the holding centre, they were mostly Croats, but there were other ethnicities as well, Slovaks and some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long they stayed there and whether they went elsewhere from there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: They stayed there briefly. After the screening, we would send some of them home immediately if their stay there was safe, and as for others, they went in two or three days, depending on the transport, either to Sremska Mitrovica, or to the camp in Begaci.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did you furnish the information you obtained in those interviews? Who did you inform about your activities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I submitted reports to my immediate superior, Captain Muncan, and Captain Muncan then compiled the information and went to brief Colonel Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who gave you your tasks?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I received my tasks from Muncan, whereas he received his tasks from Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The type of activities you performed, is that the kind of work you did while you were still active in the counter-intelligence service of the 1st Military District? Was that part of your typical activities at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you that that was my basic work. Everything begins with an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were in Sid, do you remember whether you had contacts with the security organs from the Guards Brigade, OG South, Major Sljivancanin, or any of his associates?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I don't know whether Petkovic had contacts, but I never met any of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Korica, please tell us whether at one point in time you went from Sid to the Vukovar region and, if so, when, what was the reason, and how did that come about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I think that in the evening, and possibly in the morning, in the morning, on the 19th, Captain Muncan told us to go to Negoslavci, to Colonel Mrksic in the Guards Brigade, because we were needed there in order to assist in the screening of people in Vukovar. Many people had surrendered, there were many captured persons and many refugees, and Sljivancanin alone couldn't deal with that.
