Therefore, we were attached to the group that had come from the security administration comprising Colonel Bogdan Vujic, Tomic, Kijanovic, and another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you meet with the people from the security administration there in Sid or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: We met up with these people in Negoslavci in the premises of Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember who comprised your group and how you went to Negoslavci and when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: We went to Negoslavci at night. Muncan, myself, Musesku and Radakovic were in the group. We went in the car. We arrived there at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you arrive?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: We entered the building of the command of the brigade where we found the group comprising three colonels as well as Colonel Mrksic. They were in an office. I think that it was the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell us what you remember, what took place there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Well, I remember that we sat down in several arm chairs and chairs and we all sat around a table, all of us. And then further away, on a podium, there was another table where Colonel Mrksic sat. There were maps hanging on the walls with positions marked and other items.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember what happened next? Was there a conversation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Colonel Mrksic had already started a discussion with colonels. When we arrived, we simply joined in. We sat at the table and started listening. Colonel Mrksic was telling us about the situation in Vukovar, around Vukovar, the situation in the unit, and how many people had been put out of action in the Guards Brigade. That was quite a number. I think it was around 600. He spoke for about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you see Sljivancanin, if so when, and what can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: While Colonel Mrksic spoke to us about these things, he told us to sit there and wait for Sljivancanin who was going to inform us in detail about the tasks that needed to be done. Sljivancanin came some half an hour later, maybe even more than that. He greeted all of us individually and said that he didn't have much time to socialise with us because he was in the process of talking to Vesna Bosanac who was also supposed to help us with the work that needed to be done. However, he said that the main job was at the Velepromet for that evening, and the main job that awaited us was at the hospital on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he say anything else? Did he give any other details?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: As regards that, he said that not all of us could go to the hospital because he had some men of his own and that from our group, he needed just two more men. At that moment, Colonel Vujic volunteered right away and said: I will go with Branko Korica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Just a minute, please. Based on your CV, I said and you confirmed that Bogdan Vujic was your supervisor for a while. When you met up in Negoslavci, were you on good terms? What were your relations like, given that you had worked together previously?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: My relations with Vujic were always good. First of all, he was my boss. And all of us have some complaints about our bosses, I was no exception; however, that did not sour or relations. So when we met up in Negoslavci, we greeted each other cordially, and there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Sljivancanin tell you anything about Velepromet for that evening? Was there any discussion about what needed to be done?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Yes. There was discussion about that. Sljivancanin said that Vujic and I should go together with him the following morning at 6.00, whereas everybody else would be at Velepromet. But that evening, there were things that needed to be done at Velepromet because there was a large commotion there and they expected to conduct an evacuation of the people who had arrived at Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did Sljivancanin give you, on that occasion, any details about Velepromet as to who was in charge of that facility, who had it under their control?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: He told us that that facility was the TO facility, but that there was a captain of ours there at that moment. I think it was Captain Borisavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Sljivancanin mention to you that something unpleasant could happen to you at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: No, not that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Sljivancanin mention to you on that occasion that there was a possibility of a Chetnik slaughtering and Ustasha there, or something along those lines?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: No. I was there the entire time. It's a limited area where we were, and I would have heard that, had he uttered that; however, I heard no such sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you remember whether you left that room together with Sljivancanin or did he go out first and you remained, or was it vice versa perhaps? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Sljivancanin was the first one to leave and then the rest of us got organised and went to Velepromet in two cars. I was in one car with Muncan and, the other four men were in the other car, three colonels and another man. I don't remember who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're going to turn to the events in Velepromet, but prior to that I'm going to put another question to you. When was the next time you saw Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I saw him next in the morning at around 6.00 as we were leaving to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, please, if you remember after all these years, upon arriving in Velepromet, what did you find there? What was the atmosphere like?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: The atmosphere that I came upon at Velepromet was unpleasant. There was a large commotion there. People intermingled with our men, with TO members, with women, with children. It was quite cold, especially for children. Mostly women, children, and the elderly. Later on I heard, and I didn't go to the hangars, but I heard that in the hangars there were men who needed to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, was there a meeting held at Velepromet when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I came afterwards, a bit after the car of Vujic had arrived, and they had already organised a meeting in a room, in an office where I didn't enter. Given that my boss was at the meeting, there was no need for me to go in as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say your boss, who was your boss, as you saw it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Up until that time, Muncan was my boss and then afterwards, Colonel Bogdan Vujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How come Bogdan Vujic became your boss?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Because he's a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the situation at Velepromet or the situation at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Well, both in Velepromet and at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Korica, you've already mentioned Srecko Borisavljevic, but does that name mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Yes. We were told that at Velepromet, among the members of the Territorial Defence, there is one captain of ours, too, Borisavljevic, who we found there and who was at this meeting that had been organised by Colonel Vujic, and Ljubinko Sreckovic, a member of the TO who was at Velepromet, one of the main people there, perhaps actually the man in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said Ljubinko Sreckovic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Stojanovic. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Korica, would you perhaps like to take a bit of a rest or a sip of water? No problem whatsoever, we cannot communicate directly but please tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I support you on that. This Srecko Borisavljevic, did you meet him, did you see him that evening in that area?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us what happened after that. Actually, before we go on, can you tell us what time it was roughly in the evening. You said that you arrived at night-time in Negoslavci. We have testimony and some documents here stating when it was that you were there, but can you tell us now after all these years whether it was midnight, before midnight, late at night?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: We arrived in Negoslavci in the early evening hours. And as for Velepromet, I think it was pretty late in the evening, say 9.00 or even 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what we are going to be talking about now is happening after 10.00, right? So tell us now what it is that you remember. What did you -- saw at that time in Velepromet. What was going on there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I said there was lots of commotion there and I sort of fitted into the commotion. I looked around, Velepromet, that is, observing what was going on, and there was nothing unusual in that situation. What really affected me the most was children crying. Then, I saw a room as I was walking around, in front of the hangar, towards the end, where the door was open, and I saw a group of TO men there milling about that room. As far as I could see, most of these people were drunk. I came back and informed Colonel Vujic about that; namely, that there were some suspicious people, that's the expression I used, in that room that looked like drunkards to me and perhaps they could do something. I informed him about that and he decided to go there himself. I did not accompany him. And he had a bit of a clash with these persons who indeed were drunk. One man, and later I heard that they called him Topola, figured most prominently among them, tall, dirty, unshaved, long hair, a disreputable person by anybody's standards. But he was pretty drunk. He immediately got into a conflict with Vujic because he asked that he not take his prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. You described this Topola.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you were not present there when Vujic went there. Did you hear this story from Vujic or did you see their conflict? Could you please describe, first of all, what you saw from where you were or then what you heard? So let's start from there.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: All right. I told you what you saw, what was going on inside. I went to where Vujic was, near the office. He had business to attend to there, and there were people all over the place that we contacted, and when I reported to him, he went to the actual place, but I did not see this quarrel with Topola at that moment, but Vujic told me that he had quarrelled about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did you personally see that Topola later in that area and what was he doing, if you saw him yourself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I did see Topola. I saw him myself that same evening when the buses came and when we were making lists of people on the buses. He was also by the buses where Bogdan Vujic was making these lists. And again, he asked that Vujic not take their prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, when you came there to Velepromet, what was your task? What was it that you were supposed to do? I didn't ask you that. I first wanted to hear about the atmosphere, but what was your task at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Our task in Velepromet was to organise the evacuation of persons in accordance with the number of buses that would arrive and that then these persons should be sent on to the camp in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you personally separate people there or had those people already been separated somewhere?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I personally did not separate someone, nor did I enter the hangar. These people had already been separated and that is why women, children, and the elderly were in front of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, to the best of your recollection, these people who you are just going to describe later who entered the buses, were they all in the same hangar, in one hangar? You described the room that you saw. Was it in several locations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: No, I don't remember consider that to be the hangar, this room that Vujic went to. That's a smaller room. I don't know how many hangars there were where people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the buses arrive, and what happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Well, when the buses arrived, Bogdan Vujic ordered that we write a list of the names of all the persons who entered the buses. So I was making a list of people on the last bus. People from the hangar were brought to the bus. They were all supposed to sit down and to have the bus 100 per cent full.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did these people look like to you? First of all, what gender, if we can put it that way, or can you tell us their age and what did they look like physically?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Well, physically, perhaps they were exhausted but they behaved normally. They sat down as a matter of course. There were no incidents, no nothing. No one had any bandages. I didn't see anyone injured. I personally went up to every one of them and wrote down their names and surnames. So I asked some of them why they were there, since they were, say, from Herzegovina, and this man answered me: Well, I'm wondering the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you draw any conclusions as to what the ethnicity was of these persons? You said that somebody was from Herzegovina; we know that this is not an area close to Vukovar. When you took their names, how did you find out where they were from, these people on your bus?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: On my bus, I made a list, but we were not supposed to write down anything else but the names and surnames of these persons. However, I did ask some of them, as I looked at them, I asked them where they were from. Quite a few of them were from Herzegovina, and quite a few were from behind Zagreb, even further off, towards Slovenia, and from the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you conclude what their predominant ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: For the most part, they were Croats, judging by their names and surnames.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many buses came there, in your view?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were four buses there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These buses, were they military buses and did they have any escort?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: As far as I saw, that was the first time when part of the military police came to Velepromet providing security for the buses, but before that, I did not see any soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This security provided by the military police, was that only in terms of personnel or was there something else too; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, it was personnel, and there was this security for taking the convoy there and escorting it with an armoured vehicle, a combat armoured vehicle, BOV.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Korica, do you remember this BOV arriving in front of the hangar, turning its lights on towards the hangar, did you see any such scene? Does that jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: No. No, I did not see that. I guess I would have seen the lights on. I don't know how I could not have seen something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see or hear that there were some corpses there in that area in Velepromet and around it on that evening?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: That evening I was only in Velepromet. I did not leave the Velepromet compound to view the area. But within Velepromet itself, I did not see any corpses anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that evening while you were in Velepromet, did you hear any shooting in the immediate vicinity, if I can put it that way, that would sound like shooting nearby, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Shooting nearby? I didn't hear any such thing. But there was shooting further away, most of it with tracer bullets. People were celebrating the fact that the war was over, and that was a normal thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "tracer bullets," let's be very precise. How do you see this trace, does it go up or do you see it horizontally?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: It goes up and it makes an arch.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another thing in relation to what was going on in Velepromet, did you personally hear any threats that somebody was supposed to kill the colonel there or any one of you? Did you hear any such thing there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: There were some things that were said like what Topola was saying, protests over the fact that the prisoners of war were being taken away because they thought that they belonged to them. As for threats or more serious incidents, there weren't any, not at all. I did not hear anyone say to anybody else that he was supposed to kill him or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear from Vujic that somebody threatened him that way at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear about anything like that from Vujic either. Then in Belgrade, we're neighbours, and he told me some things that I had not heard but he was convincing me that I had heard them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll deal with that later. Tell me -- just a moment, please. You said that this Topola and these territorials had something to say. Do you remember what it was that they were saying? What was it that they wanted; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I don't know what his intention was later but what he was asking for was that the prisoners remain there, that we should not take them away. That they would judge them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Were you there -- or, rather, were the buses filled up and what happened then?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: All the buses were filled up and their police commander, I think it was a captain, he gave instructions to every soldier who was behind the driver on every one of the buses what to do during the ride if the people who were being transported start protesting or if they start rocking the bus, because the bus could fall over if they did that. Then the buses left with a vehicle in front of them and an armoured vehicle behind them and they went in the direction of Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood this, were there soldiers or military policemen on these buses, on all the buses?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Military policemen were on every one of the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Two on my bus. I didn't see how many there were in the other buses and they were right behind the drivers. As we were boarding the buses, they were at the door and nobody else could enter the bus, the buses, only those who were boarding the buses and we who were making the lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us another thing: What did you do with these lists of these people that you had compiled on the bus?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: As for the list that I compiled on the bus, since Bogdan Vujic was still writing up the list of his bus, I handed my list over to Srecko Borisavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During that stay there, and before the buses were boarded and as they were boarded, was Borisavljevic with you and what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Borisavljevic was with us that evening. I think he was there the entire evening, but he also had other things to attend to, and he continuously went here and there. He went to the office, he received reports, requests from the town, so he was dealing with the current issues and wasn't very actively involved in boarding the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you be able to specify approximately what time it was when the buses left the Velepromet, were you still there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I was there when the buses left Velepromet, which was either midnight or even after midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay there and where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: We stayed there briefly. After the men left the hangar, we first took women and children into hangars and I think that Srecko organised for water to be brought to them because children asked for water so that they could spend the night indoors because it was quite cold outside. It was November, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember Vujic and his group with Kijanovic and Tomic, did they remain there until the end? Do you remember them being there when the buses left?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Vujic was definitely there. As for Kijanovic and the other two, I'm not sure that they remained until the end. But I think that all of them left together to Negoslavci, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you go back to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I went back to Negoslavci with my group, and in our vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: We went again to the same building, to the same room from where we had gone to Colonel Mrksic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you be more specific about the time? I'm trying not to be too demanding on you, I know it's been 15 years, you don't have to be fully accurate if you are unable to.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I'm not able to be fully accurate, but I think that it was after 1.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did you find there, upon entering that room?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I think that when we came to that room, Colonel Mrksic was no longer there. Rather, there was a duty officer or duty operations officer. I'm not sure about that. We sat there, Vujic came after us, but I think that Kijanovic and Tomic had already arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You think that Kijanovic and Tomic were already there and that Vujic came after you? Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I think that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you do next? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: We went to the basement where they offered us something to eat. Some people took a can, some didn't, and then we went back and sat in the office in those same chairs where we had sat earlier. And we stayed there until the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I take it that you spent the entire night in that room sleeping, if you slept at all?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Some people slept. I may have slept half an hour to an hour, not longer than that. I slept in an upright position, sitting in a chair, and it wasn't very comfortable. And the chair wasn't as comfortable as this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Vujic, was he there with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: We were there together the whole time. There was nowhere else to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you earlier and I'll ask you again whether there, that night, upon your return from Velepromet, you saw Veselin Sljivancanin anywhere there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I'm sure that I didn't see him until I left for the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember perhaps seeing another tall officer that evening whom you hadn't seen earlier?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: In the course of the night, a bit later, General Jerko Crmaric came. I asked him why he had come because he also used to be a chief, and he said that he came to see what buses and transportation means were needed in order to evacuate the people. At that point in time, he was the logistics commander of the 1st Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, during the discussion that was held when you arrived in Negoslavci and met with Mrksic and then Sljivancanin came, was it discussed at all what was to be done at the hospital on the following day, what tasks were to be performed by security organs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Sljivancanin told us that that was the main task for us for the following day and that we would be conducting screening in the hospital and that we would send some people to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: He said that it was because there were many people there who had taken shelter in the hospital and didn't go to the Velepromet compound when they were told that they could go there. He said that there were some members of the ZNG, of MUP, and that there were work criminals who had taken shelter in the hospital and camouflaged themselves in doctor's uniforms. He said that those people needed to be separated and that everything needed to be cleared at the hospital and prepared for the arrival of the International Red Cross so as to avoid any incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were these people supposed to be taken?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: These people, at least that's what Sljivancanin told us, were supposed to be taken to Sremska Mitrovica, just like those from Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Now let us turn to the morning of the 20th, what happened then? Did you leave Negoslavci, who was with you, and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: From what you're saying, you're now moving on to quite a different topic. I think this is probably a good time for a break, and it will give Mr. Korica a chance for a little rest. So we will adjourn now for 20 minutes and resume at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Korica, we are now up to the 20th in the morning. Let us be more specific, where did you spend the entire night? Was it in that building that you called the command building?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Yes, we were in that building and we were in the same room where we had first come in after arriving from Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now let us turn to the 20th in the morning. What do you remember? Where did you go? Who went with you? What time of the day it was? Do you remember any of those things?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: In the morning at around 6.00, we left from Negoslavci to the hospital in a military vehicle with Mr. Sljivancanin, Mr. Vujic, myself, a captain - I don't know his name - and another individual, fifth individual, I don't know who he was. We set out towards the hospital. It was still dark. We drove slowly. Perhaps we stopped in two or three locations, but I don't know why we stopped because I was in the back of the vehicle. We went straight to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened when you reached the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: As we were driving towards the hospital, Sljivancanin told us in the car in greater detail what we were supposed to do at the hospital, saying that we could perhaps need to stay longer because, as far as I understood, Vesna Bosanac had not made a list of the hospital staff so that needed to be done. Once the hospital staff was separated from those who were not members of the staff, we were supposed to conduct triage of those who belonged to neither of those groups and were also neither wounded nor sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you came to the hospital, did you enter the building? Did you start with your work right away?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: When we came to the hospital, Mr. Sljivancanin went inside. I stayed back -- I don't think that any of us entered the building. I stayed outside of the entrance and I could see Sljivancanin through the glass. I think that he stood on an elevated object and the hospital staff stood around him. He spoke to them, most likely about this need to separate themselves from the others. Once Sljivancanin concluded, we entered in order to start our work. Bogdan Vujic and I came in. We were to do the same kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, did anybody else arrive at the hospital with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: No, nobody arrived with us, but while we were there, four or five officers arrived. They came in. I didn't even know who they were. Later I heard that those were our doctors who had arrived in order to assist in technical/professional matters, to conduct the triage of the patients in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you entered the hospital, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: When we entered the hospital, Vujic went to one side, I went to the right. We went from one bed to the next one. Next to me was a person who was previously employed in the hospital and who knew a lot of people, and if somebody was in bed and wasn't actually wounded or sick, I would take that person outside to the front of the hospital. That was the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How could you tell whether somebody was wounded or not, the people that you inspected?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Well, I talked to them. I asked them whether they had been wounded or were sick. One of them even said that he was wounded. I asked him to show me and he rolled up his sleeve a bit and he had a scratch just a few centimetres long; it wasn't even bandaged. I told him to get up. Once he got up, I could tell that he could stand perfectly normally. I turned over the pillow and -- on his bed and I could see a hand-grenade under the pillow. I told him, I asked him: What's this? He said: I have no idea. I didn't have any time to discuss it any longer with him. I simply took him outside, and there were already people out there who, pursuant to Sljivancanin's request, had gone out on their own because they were neither members of the hospital staff nor wounded, and they left the building pursuant to his request. And in front of the emergency room, women stood on one side, so I didn't take them out. Men were on the other side next to the hospital wall. They all came up to the table, to this one table where the military police had organised a search. I handed them over to them, and then I returned to the hospital to get the others. Sometimes I'd take one person out, sometimes two, sometimes even three people at a time. At any rate, they were all men, healthy, able-bodied, and I think I took about 20 of them out that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what did you do when somebody lay in bed in plaster, in bandages. When somebody was truly a patient, a sick person, a wounded person, what did you do in that situation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: In that situation, Sljivancanin told us that we had nothing to do with the wounded, that they would be dealt with by professionals and that professionals would examine them to see whether they were wounded or sick or not. I assume that this was done by the doctors who came from the Novi Sad hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These doctors who came, were they in uniform, these people from Novi Sad, were they military or civilian doctors, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they were officers, military physicians, military doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was Vujic doing during that period of time; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I'm telling you, I went to one side, Vujic went to the other side, and we worked independently of each other, and we did exactly the same type of work, and we came across each other as we took people out. He took people out, I took people out, and then we'd go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many people Vujic took out that way, as you did?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I cannot say because I really do not know. But he took out quite a few people. I don't think that I took out more than he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you do when you'd come across a person who was a civilian who had not been wounded, not sick, who was just standing there? Were there such situations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Yes, there were such situations. I would ask that person who worked at the hospital whether this individual was an employee of the hospital, medical staff or non-medical staff, and then he'd say no, and then I'd ask if he had an ID, and then if he'd say no, then I'd take him out too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was your boss there? Who was it that instructed you what to do? Whose orders did you carry out? Who did you obey?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Colonel Bogdan Vujic at Velepromet and in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you see where these people were taken out once they were taken to the entrance to the hospital? Did you see what happened to them after that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I just saw them while they were in front of the hospital lined up, as I already told you, and I really don't know whether they went to the main gate, whether they went to some other area, or to the buses, which I did not see at all. That's what Vujic asked me in Belgrade, too, whether I saw how many buses there were behind the hospital. I told him that I did not see the buses, and he said: Well, how was it that you didn't see the buses? And I said: Well, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did Vujic ask you that in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Oh, say a year later. He was chasing me around the marketplace and -- all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now that we are dealing with this area, did Vujic tell you that he had talked to The Hague OTP? Did you hear about that from him? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: He saw me a few times in a cafe, here and there and everywhere, and ultimately he managed to take me to his home, although I had refused until then. It's not far away from my apartment. When we came to his home, he showed me a statement that he had given to an investigator from The Hague. Then he started reading it out sentence by sentence. I know -- well, he said: "When I first came to Velepromet, I found Branko Korica there sitting in an armchair and holding a rifle on his knees." And I said: Bogdan, don't you understand that I never had a rifle or any kind of long-barreled weapon. I have an ID for the front line that says exactly what kind of weapon I have. And I still have the originals of those IDs. And it says exactly what motor vehicle I use, what direction I go in, and what weapon I have. Otherwise, I could not pass any check-point. And the question is what would happen if someone established that I had something that was not recorded there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. When you talked to Bogdan Vujic, how did he react to your information? Did he accept what you were saying as accurate? Did he oppose what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I remember he said --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just respectfully ask my learned friend if he'd be kind enough just to tell me exactly where there is in the proofing notes. There have been two other areas which I let go past, but I don't see this in this proofing note at all. Perhaps it's my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last sentence in the proofing notes is Vujic also showed him his statement that he had given to the OTP from The Hague and he asked Korica to confirm the accuracy of that statement. That is my last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, with the utmost respect, that is just one particular line. My learned friend is now going into the minutiae or the detail of it, and with the utmost respect, I would ask that that should have been clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean -- well, just tell us that, Mr. Korica. Do you remember how Mr. Vujic reacted when he talked to you about these recollections of Vukovar when you were presenting your own recollections, how did he react?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: He asked me for several pieces of concrete information, and I believe that he changed his statement then. But he says that it didn't matter what he wrote, what he said, and I said that it mattered to me, that it was important for me because I cannot go to Croatia to visit my father's grave and my mother's grave because of that rifle. So that is very important to me whether he said that before this court. But there were these other things, too, that I did not agree with at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How come you have this information that he testified before this court?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I have this colleague who is retired, he retired early, and he was telling his friends that he watched a direct broadcast from The Hague when Bogdan Vujic testified. Well, he was probably exaggerating, but he said that in every other sentence, he said: Branko Korica saw this. Branko Korica heard this. Branko Korica told me this and that. And many other things. As a matter of fact, even that I was his security in the war, and then they were teasing me as to why it was that I went to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just my last question, I'm not going to deal with this any longer: What did you mean when you said "how would I go to my father's and my mother's grave"? So why did that affect you, that Vujic mentioned your name?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Well, I was in Vukovar. I was in the war operations zone, but I did not take part in war operations, and I did not have a long-barreled weapon, a rifle. I know that the president of the State of Croatia said that he could forgive everyone everything but he could forgive no one for Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on. We'll go back to the subject that we had dealt with before. Mr. Korica, do you remember, can you tell us how many people were out in that corridor separated, to the best of your recollection, roughly? I'm not asking you for an exact figure.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I took out 20 and a bit more, and then in terms of what I saw, I assume that Bogdan Vujic did the same thing. I guess it was about 60, 70 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I asked you but perhaps I didn't, who searched them, who frisked them? Did you see?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: They were frisked by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you do with this grenade that you had found?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I handed it over to the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Vujic find anything?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I didn't see that he found anything. I know that he was carrying around this helmet as a memento.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, what you did within the hospital, how long did it go on for?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Well, it went on for about two hours, perhaps a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you finished that, did you stay on at the hospital or did you leave? Do you remember what happened then?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Then, when we finished that, the observers had already arrived, the European monitors, that is, and Mr. Sljivancanin was talking to them. I passed by them, and I came across Bogdan Vujic by the gate. We stood there for a bit, and then a military vehicle came by, it was going to Negoslavci. We got a ride with them to Velepromet and that's how we returned to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just two more questions, brief ones, in relation to the hospital. As you were carrying out this triage, as we've been calling it here, this work at the hospital, did you see whether anybody was carried out of the hospital on a stretcher in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I did not come across anyone on a stretcher in the hospital, and I didn't see anything like that outside either. In all fairness, I did not walk all around the hospital to see. But on this side where we were taking people out, it is certain that there were no stretchers there, no beds, no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In that group that you took out, and those who were standing out there, did you see anybody with crutches?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And another question: After the moment you saw Sljivancanin in front of the hospital, and in relation to the other places that we are going to talk about now where you were on that day, did you see Sljivancanin at any of these places later during the course of that day?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I saw Sljivancanin then in front of the hospital as he was talking to the monitors, and after that, I did not see him again, throughout my stay in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us proceed with your stay in Vukovar. So you went to Velepromet and what happened then?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Bogdan Vujic and I went to an office. I don't know whether that's Borisavljevic's office or Ljubinko Stojanovic's office. I think it's Ljubinko's office. Vujic sat at the desk taking some notes, and I sat on the side because Borisavljevic brought me this briefcase and said that his soldier, a policeman, found that somewhere behind the hangar. He handed that briefcase over to me and said: You're going to be the first person going to Belgrade, so hand this in at the security administration. I opened the briefcase, and I saw that there were a few wallets inside and perhaps two envelopes and some paper. First I thought that some of the TO members wanted to plant this on me in order to compromise us. I took one of these wallets, got an ID card out of it, and I wrote down all the information contained in the ID. I also made a list of all the documents that were in the wallet, who this belonged to. When there was money, I wrote that down, too, the actual currency and the number of each bank note. So that's exactly what I did. I wrote all of that down and then returned it into the briefcase that was supposed to be taken to the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was Vujic there and, if so, what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Vujic was there, just a metre away from me at this biggish desk or table, and I was sitting at this small table sitting in a chair and I was doing all of this, whereas he was sitting at this desk and writing something, but I don't know what it was that he was writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: As we did that, at one moment, a military policeman came in and said: Comrade-colonel, Arkan has entered his compound with his people. He forced his way in. Vujic sent a soldier to bring Arkan into the office. After some time, he came back and said: Comrade-colonel, Arkan refuses to come in. He wants you to go and see him. Vujic was upset and he raised his voice, saying to the military policeman: Go get military police and bring him in. The soldier left and even before he returned, Arkan came into the office. He went straight to the desk of colonel, he sat across from him. He put his automatic rifle on the desk and then he leaned over his rifle, and he said: What do you want, colonel? And without waiting for an answer, he continued: You are crazy, colonel. You are just an ordinary fool. Knowing Vujic, I thought that an incident would break out; however, that didn't happen. Vujic simply said to him: What are you doing here? Do you want to kill here as well? Since they argued quite passionately, I wanted to reduce the tension and disrupt their dialogue. I addressed Arkan by his last name, and I said: Raznjatovic, I know you and you don't know me. I tricked him there. I told him that I worked for the Ministry of the Interior and I told him even which building. And then I asked him: Do you know where that building is? And he said yes. Then I told him: If you expel a single Croat here, Tudjman will expel five of my people from Croatia. If you expel one village here, or kill people in one village, Tudjman will kill people in five villages of my people, because all of my people are in Croatia. So who am I to fight against, against you or Tudjman? He removed himself from the table and said: I'm not the one doing the killing. And then Vujic continued arguing with him and said: It is your people who are killing. Then Arkan stopped him and once again said to him: Colonel, you're crazy. Come to the other office in an hour, a cabinet session will be held here, cabinet session of the SAO Krajina and then you will see what decisions will be taken. Vujic replied: I will certainly come.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Let us conclude with this portion and then we'll proceed. Had you seen Arkan ever prior to that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I had never seen Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: His presence and the dialogue which took place, were you afraid upon hearing it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: No, there was no reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did Vujic appear to you? You knew him well. Did he appear to be frightened?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Vujic does have these outbursts, especially when he gets upset. Arkan didn't show any aggressiveness. I spoke completely normally to him. I had occasion to speak to him once again, but not on that day. He went there and I don't know whether there was any danger. I simply turned my head to the other side and continued working as though Arkan wasn't there at all. Had there been any more serious problems, I probably would have done something to protect both Vujic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell us what happened next.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: After some time, after less than an hour, another person came in, a colonel this time, a tall man wearing a military uniform with epaulets and rank insignia hanging down his shoulder, down his sleeve. And straight from the door, he asked: Who is Colonel Branko? Vujic answered: I am. He said: Arkan is inviting you to come and attend the cabinet session. Arkan, when sending this colonel, must have said that he was looking for a colonel, and Vujic introduced himself as Branko so he mixed up that, and from that time on, Vujic has been known as Colonel Branko.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. You worked actively with him in your previous army service. Did he ever previously introduce himself to anyone as Colonel Branko?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Definitely not. I know him very well. I'm positive that he never did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Did Vujic object to going? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: No. Vujic got up immediately and went with the colonel to that other office where the cabinet session was held. Since the door was closed, I couldn't see the persons who went in to attend the session. So Vujic went to the cabinet session and the other colonel remained standing outside, guarding the door until the session was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, did Vujic ask you to come with him to the cabinet session for any reason at all?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: God forbid, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell me what happened next.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I continued doing my work. Vujic returned from the cabinet session; that didn't take long. He returned from the session and told me about the main things that were decided at the session. I know that he told me that Arkan was the only one who was armed in that room, and that he didn't take part in the work of the cabinet session. Second, he told me that he argued with the cabinet members, even with Goran Hadzic, about incidents that he heard had occurred, even some killings. I didn't see it myself. And also some incidents involving prisoners, because Goran Hadzic asked from Vujic that the prisoners from the hospital be surrendered to him. Vujic said that he informed him that he wasn't competent to hand over prisoners to anyone, including him. Hadzic replied to him: Anyway, we don't need the army. We don't need Serbia. We organised this rebellion. We won our victory, and the prisoners are all ours. If you fail to give us the prisoners, we will attack the JNA tanks, and if that doesn't help, we will throw ourselves under the tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Earlier, when you described the meeting with Arkan, you retold us the dialogue as to who said what. Can I inquire how come you remember in such a great detail who said what?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I thought it was funny. It was funny to observe Vujic in that situation, and I must have told this to my colleagues in Belgrade at least 100 times, and I repeated it I don't know how many times, so my recollection of this is very vivid. This is how come I could tell you about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, did Vujic tell you how the meeting, how the cabinet session ended?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: He told me that the session ended and that there was something that he didn't like about it either. Halfway through the session, as they were debating, some lieutenant-colonel entered the room. He didn't know what his name was or the unit that he had come from. He didn't know whether he was from Belgrade or Negoslavci. He handed in a dispatch, a telegram, or he told Goran Hadzic that he had received an approval to establish a camp for war prisoners should the cabinet decide so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened then. Was that the end of the meeting or did it continue?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: No, that was the end of the cabinet session. They came out into the Velepromet compound, at one point even I came out, and I recognised only Arkan and Goran Hadzic among them. I didn't know other people. He talked to the TO members who approached him to greet him. Ljubinko Stojanovic was there because they used to work together at Velepromet, so there were many people that he used to know there as a businessman. I went back into the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to Vujic; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I don't know where the entire cabinet went, or some individual cabinet members. I don't even know where Arkan went. Vujic and I remained together at Velepromet. But at some point in the afternoon, he said that he was going to the barracks to have lunch. He went to the barracks and we didn't see each other until we met in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That morning when you left from Negoslavci to the hospital, what happened to the other people in your group? Did you see that or did you hear about that? I'm referring to Muncan and other people in your group.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I later heard that Muncan and my group, and I think even Kijanovic and Tomic, that they went to Velepromet and worked there as long as there was work to do because they needed to send off some transports to Croatia. There were complications. These transports returned because the Croats refused to take them in and so on. And then all of them went to the barracks, so they were in the barracks until the evening, whereas I remained at Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you meet up with the rest of the men from your group?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: We met up towards the evening when Muncan and the rest of my group came in a car to fetch me in Velepromet. We got into the car and then we went straight to Sid. However, en route, Muncan said that the prisoners from the barracks had been transferred to Ovcara. And he said that we were to go to Ovcara to observe the situation there, to see whether there was any chance of interviewing any of those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Before we turn to that portion of your evidence, tell us this, please: Muncan and the others from your group who were separated from you during the day, did they tell you about what had happened in the barracks? Did they give you any details?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Yes, they told me -- I heard that there were incidents in the barracks. Muncan told me. Apparently there were attacks on the buses and that the people who were outside were pointing to the people on the buses saying: He killed this member of my family. He killed that member of my family. So there was a lot of intimidation and they had to increase security detail, and then the situation calmed down and then they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you met with Muncan, in the course of two previous days, did you ever hear Ovcara being mentioned? Did anybody mention Ovcara prior to that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Until Muncan said in the car that we were going to Ovcara, I didn't even know what Ovcara was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. So did you get to Ovcara, to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: We came to the hangar from the lower side, if I may call it that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. You will describe to us -- what time of the day it was? Was it day or night?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: It was neither, neither day or night. It was just before dusk, but it was still -- there was still more daylight than darkness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: We came close to the entrance to the hangar. We drove up in our car and we halted and then Muncan and Pero Musesku left the car, and they said to me and Radakovic to wait in the car. They went to the hangar, Muncan and Musesku, and I think that they came back within five minutes. Muncan said: Start the car. Let us leave. There are no conditions here for us to do anything. They don't have a separate room for us to work and it's getting dark. We are running out of time. We'll do this another time. We went straight to Sid without stopping at the command of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Did Muncan tell you of any other details, what he saw in the hangar, or was it only what you said just now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: He didn't say anything else to me except for the fact that there were no conditions for us to do any work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, can you tell us what the atmosphere in front of the hangar was like, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: In front of the door of the hangar, I saw a policeman, by who they went and went into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "policeman."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I mean military policeman. Then about 5 or 6 metres away from him, there were two military policemen who were sort of talking. I don't know whether they were on duty. And about 20 metres away, behind a little shed or a little pre-fabricated building, there was a group of officers standing there and soldiers, too, who were talking normally. I didn't see anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see any territorials, as we call them here, anybody else? Were there any other people there in uniform walking around?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I can tell you that as for the road that we took as we got there in this car there was no one there, and in that group, I don't know who the territorials were and who the soldiers were and who the active-duty officers were, and whether there were any territorials behind them on the other side, the upper side. I didn't get out of the car, so that's what I managed to see from the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does this jog your memory: Were there any buses there perhaps?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: No. No. I could not see any buses in terms of everything that I managed to see from the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. You said that you were there only about five minutes altogether, so that was a short period of time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: From there, we went by car directly to Sid. We were billeted in a private apartment, our group, that is, and we were near the post office. So Muncan brought us to our building, parked the car, and that's where we all got out, whereas Muncan went to the post office on foot to report to Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic, an oral report, that is. As for the written report, he wrote that up later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you write any reports, do you remember, in relation to those two days of work there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I didn't write anything, but I participated and told Muncan about everything I did. I reported to him and also what was of interest there. Bogdan Vujic was with me all the time, and we were exchanging information. We were telling each other things all the time. So it wasn't necessary to submit a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay on there in Sid, Mr. Korica, can you tell us approximately, after this 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: We stayed at least for another ten days or so, perhaps even more than that, and then we moved to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long were you in Vukovar and what did you do there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: We were in Vukovar -- well, I was there until the 15th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you do, what was your work there, if you can tell us very briefly.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: We worked on many things, particularly collecting documentation about crimes that had been committed in Vukovar, in villages. We conducted interviews with persons who were of interest to us, both of Serb and Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. During that period of your activity in Vukovar, did you go to the Vukovar Hospital, and did you conduct the same kind of interviews there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I went to the Vukovar Hospital quite a few times. I conducted quite a few interviews with the hospital staff, both Serbs and Croats. There were quite a few nurses who had stayed on in the hospital, who remained working in the hospital. So there were things of interest there, but there were more things of interest around Vukovar and different documents, Mercep and other leading people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell us, do you remember whether near the Vukovar hospital, you found something that was interesting for you in terms of your operative work, some things, some premises?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: We received some information to the effect that opposite the hospital, across the street near the hospital, there is a watchmaker's shop, and next to the shop a new little house was being built. And underneath the window of that house, we were told to dig and that we would find weapons and a notebook that contains the minefields in Vukovar. We did that and we found that and we immediately handed over that notebook to Colonel Basic, and he was an engineering officer and he was working on the mop-up of the area, sanitization of the terrain. But we also found a radio there; that was the communications centre. Our experts dismantled that. As far as I heard as they were working there, they had never discovered that radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How far away is that from the yard of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: I think, say, 30 to 40 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Korica, in that period while you were in Vukovar, it's almost three months, as far as I can see, did you receive any information? Did you hear anything about what was going on in Ovcara, about the crime in Ovcara, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Afterwards, I did, but I stayed in Vukovar for a long time and I went to the hospital many times, and even in the hospital, no one, absolutely no one was talking about that, about those persons being killed. I heard in Belgrade, say a year after that, from the media, that that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just give me a brief answer, not to go into all the details. During this period while you were there, in the hospital, were there ethnic Serbs and Croats who worked there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Quite a few Serbs and Croats, quite a few. I don't know who was the head nurse at the hospital before, but after this evacuation, the head nurse of the hospital was a Croat lady from a neighbouring village of mine, near my village in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question. We heard testimony here that some lieutenant wanted to assassinate Mr. Vujic with a sniper on that day, the 20th in the hospital. Do you know about any kind of assassination attempt against Colonel Branko's life?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Now I understand. Two months after that, I had this situation, as it were, that was reminiscent of that as I was in the cellar of the hospital as I was conducting interviews, and then Pero Musesku came to interview these persons, and then the person who came in said: Where's Branko? And he said: Well, he's on another assignment. A person we know well. An officer, an NCO. And he kept saying: Where's Branko, where's Branko? He insisted. And he: Well, he's doing something different now. And then he said: Well, where? And since they were on pretty good terms, he managed to learn from him that some people had sent him to liquidate me, to kill me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Branko Korica?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA
utterances.text: Yes, Branko Korica, who he knew well. And I told Bogdan Vujic about this, say a year after that, and it's only if he ascribed that to himself. I mean, I haven't got anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have concluded the examination-in-chief of this witness and I have no further questions, and I think that this would be an ideal moment to adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Vasic, do you plan to ask any questions of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I do have some questions. I don't think I can do much in two or three remaining minutes, so I support what Mr. Lukic said, and as in the past, I will try to consolidate my questions and to reduce them to a minimum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We adjourn now until 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of November, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
